sources.title: Pedestrian Comfort Guidance for London (Pedestrian Comfort Level Guidance, First Edition)
sources.extract: Text extracted locally this round. Scope: footways and crossings. Crowding = people per hour / 60 / clear footway width, calculated for average flow, peak-hour flow and an Average of Maximum Activity check (busiest 10-second samples, built into TfL's spreadsheet). Figure 8 bands: A+ under 3, A 3-5, A- 6-8, B+ 9-11 (recommended minimum for all area types), B 12-14, B- 15-17, C+ 18-20, C 21-23, C- 24-26, D 27-35, E over 35 ppmm. Figure 9 rates acceptability by area type (High Street, Office and Retail, Residential, Tourist, Transport Interchange), peak versus Average of Maximum; B is acceptable at peak on High Street and 'at risk' elsewhere in the text extraction (cell-level reading to be confirmed by two users). PCL should not fall below C+ at peak even where vitality compensates.

sources.title: Commute Trip Reduction, TDM Encyclopedia
sources.extract: Re-opened. Ewing 1993 Sacramento model: 100% transit/rideshare subsidy predicted -35% CBD commute travel, 50% subsidy -20% (predicted, no stated baseline). Spack and Finkelstein 2014 (Minneapolis-St Paul, measured): TDM buildings generate 34-37% less traffic than ITE average rates and need 17-24% fewer parking spaces. Rye 2002 and Boarnet et al. 2014: comprehensive worksite programmes cut peak auto trips 4-20%; without financial incentives usually under 10%. Best Workplaces for Commuters survey (Denver, Houston, San Francisco, Washington DC): about 15% with incentives, about 7% services and information only.

modules.name: Person-trip generation and mode split
modules.effort: M (about 2 weeks; loading and documenting baselines by trip end dominates; MVP is the static table without Monte Carlo)
modules.design_question: How many person-trips will the program generate per day and in the peak hour, by use, purpose and mode, using a mode split that matches each use's trip end?
inputs: Layer 0: GFA by program tag (office, residential, hotel, retail, cultural/civic, public, amenity)
Layer 0: dwelling units, unit mix, hotel keys
Baseline mode-share table loaded by the user, one row per trip end (residence, origin, destination) with source, year, sample size, confidence interval and date accessed
Optional SITE output: distance to nearest rapid-transit station
Optional scenario: event or weekend profile (BC Place, Entertainment District)

parameters.name: GFA per use (Layer 0)
parameters.relationship: More office or retail GFA raises employees and visitors, so daily person-trips rise roughly in proportion. More residential GFA raises resident trips through persons per unit.

parameters.name: Floor area per employee
parameters.relationship: Lower area per job (denser office) raises employee count and commute trips for the same GFA. No Vancouver value was sourced, so it is an editable team assumption.

parameters.name: Baseline trip end (residence, origin or destination)
parameters.relationship: Resident trips use residence-based shares. Office, retail, hotel and civic attraction trips need destination-based shares. A residence-based share applied to attractions overstates walking and understates regional auto and transit, so the tool shows a red badge and blocks the result.

parameters.name: Trip rate per person, unit or room by purpose
parameters.relationship: Higher rates scale every downstream flow linearly. Resident rates can come from the residence-based Trip Diary; attraction rates need destination data. Dashboard values must be loaded by hand.

parameters.name: Internal capture between uses (default OFF in CBD mode)
parameters.relationship: Zone shares already include short walks between nearby uses, so removing internal trips first double-discounts external trips. Switch on only in an ITE vehicle-trip pathway with NCHRP 684 pair rates (not opened).

parameters.name: Mode split vector by purpose and trip end
parameters.relationship: Moving share from auto driver to walk or transit lowers vehicle trips, parking demand and kerb pressure but raises station and footway flows, which feed P09-M03 and P09-M04.

parameters.name: Distance to nearest rapid-transit stop
parameters.relationship: The VTPI table (Vernez Moudon and Stewart 2013) prints +0.15 for walking and +0.29 for transit against distance, contradicting expectation. Show the printed sign; any direction rule is a labelled team assumption in sensitivity runs only.

parameters.name: Land-use mix and street connectivity
parameters.relationship: Higher mix and intersection density are associated with more walking (elasticities 0.15 and 0.39) and less vehicle travel (-0.09 and -0.12). Use as sensitivity tests, not stacked multipliers.

parameters.name: Parking supply per use (from P09-M02)
parameters.relationship: Fewer or priced stalls lower drive-alone share; parking-management measures typically cut requirements 10-30% each in car-oriented contexts. Treat as a scenario, not a default.

parameters.name: Auto occupancy
parameters.relationship: Higher occupancy turns the same auto-person trips into fewer vehicle trips. No sourced local value; editable team assumption.

parameters.name: Peak-hour share of daily trips (K) and directional split
parameters.relationship: A higher K raises station, entry and kerb loads. Office is inbound in the AM and residential outbound, so the governing direction differs by use. Default K is a team assumption; the 15-minute PHF is set in P09-M04 and P09-M08.

parameters.name: Event or weekend profile
parameters.relationship: Event crowds and weekend visitors to cultural and public uses add walk and transit trips outside the weekday-only diary and shift the peak away from commute hours. No sourced rate; scenario input only.

metrics.name: Baseline-basis check (trip end)
metrics.good: Every use runs on a share whose basis matches its trip end (residence for residents; destination, place-of-work or cordon for attractions)
metrics.bad: Any attraction use on a residence-based share: red badge and attraction results suppressed
metrics.applicability_status: source-stated (S15 sampling and weighting by residence)
metrics.basis: Corrects the assumption that CBD sub-region 21/22 diary shares apply to all uses. Sub-regions have a few hundred sample households each.
metrics.method: Compare each loaded row's basis field with the use's trip end; show sample size and confidence interval beside every share.

metrics.name: Sustainable-mode share (walk + bike + transit) versus loaded baseline of the same trip end
metrics.good: At or above the loaded baseline share for that trip end
metrics.bad: Below the Metro Vancouver average share of the same survey year (value to be loaded)
metrics.basis: Data exist in the TransLink dashboard and, for destinations, in Census or cordon sources, but numbers could not be read.
metrics.method: Compare modelled share with the loaded baseline row; show basis, year and sample size.

metrics.name: Sustainable-mode share versus City target (context only)
metrics.good: Shown against the target with its year and scope; no pass/fail
metrics.bad: No fail threshold: the target is city-wide, not a site test (50% preset removed)
metrics.value_status: unverified (Transportation 2040 and climate plan not opened; two-thirds recalled)
metrics.basis: Reviewer notes Transportation 2040 set its target for 2040 and a later plan reportedly moved two-thirds to 2030. 1997 plan targets in Memon 2009 are historical.
metrics.method: Plot modelled share beside the target with target year, scope and a source badge.

metrics.name: Auto-driver share of office commute trips
metrics.good: 25% or less (about one in four, the 1997 downtown planning basis)
metrics.bad: Above 40% (editable preset)
metrics.basis: Good value is the 1997 Transportation Plan basis reported by Memon (2009), possibly superseded. Bad value is a preset. Compare against a destination-based baseline.
metrics.method: Auto-driver commute trips divided by office commute trips.

metrics.name: Internal capture share of all trips (ITE pathway only)
metrics.good: Inside the NCHRP 684 pair ranges for the use mix (ranges to be loaded)
metrics.bad: Above the upper bound of those ranges (over-claiming); any non-zero value in CBD person-trip mode
metrics.basis: Default OFF in CBD mode to avoid double-discounting; method calibrated for ITE vehicle trips.
metrics.method: Internal trips divided by total trips from the pair matrix.

visualization: Stacked bars of daily external person-trips by mode for each use, with the loaded baseline of the matching trip end drawn as a tick on each bar and a red outline where the basis mismatches
24-hour stacked area of person-trips by mode with the peak hour shaded, an in/out toggle and a dashed weekend or event overlay
Sankey from use to purpose to mode; link width is trips; hover shows factor value, source badge, basis, sample size and status colour (verified, team assumption, FALSE ASSUMPTION)

Gauge of sustainable share with baseline mark and city-target context mark; the band is labelled 'scenario spread from assumed ranges' and greyed when more than half the factor ranges are team assumptions
outputs: PersonTripTable (use x purpose x mode x hour, in/out, with basis tag per row)
PeakHourDemand {transit_in/out, walk_in/out, bike, auto_driver, taxi_TNC, servicing_vehicles}
ModeShareSummary with provenance, basis and sample size per factor
ParkingDemandEstimate (auto-driver commuters x occupancy) for P09-M02 and P09-M07
modules.method: 1) Daily person-trips per use T = driver x rate, where the driver is employees (GFA / m2 per job), residents (units x persons per unit), occupied hotel keys, or programmed visitors for civic and public uses. 2) Pick the mode-share row by trip end: residence-based Trip Diary shares (sub-regions 21 and 22) for residents; destination-based shares (Census place of work, City cordon counts, or a dashboard destination filter) for attractions. A missing or mismatched basis blocks the run. 3) Internal capture is OFF by default; optional ON only in an ITE vehicle-trip pathway. 4) Auto-driver trips = auto-person trips / occupancy. 5) Peak hour = daily x K x directional split. 6) Optional 1,000-draw Monte Carlo over low, base and high values gives a spread labelled 'scenario spread from assumed ranges'. Every factor shows source id, basis, sample size and status colour.
modules.human_judgment: Choice of benchmark zone and basis for each use; whether to claim a better split than the baseline; attendance assumptions for civic, cultural, public and event-day uses that have no standard rate; the narrative linking mode split to design moves.
modules.limits: The Trip Diary samples households by residence (a few hundred target households per CBD sub-region), so it cannot give workplace-attraction splits; Census place-of-work data are 2021 and COVID-affected. The survey is weekday-only and publishes no trips per m2. ITE rates are paywalled; recent editions reportedly carry urban-setting and person-trip data (not opened). Shares are zone averages; post-2023 change is not reflected.

parameters.name: Minimum off-street parking
parameters.relationship: No minimum applies downtown (since 2018) or citywide (since 30 June 2024), so supplying fewer stalls cannot create a by-law deficiency. Accessible and visitor stalls still count.

parameters.name: Downtown maximum (non-residential; residential row if any)
parameters.relationship: More non-residential GFA raises the permitted ceiling in proportion; stalls above it need a relaxation. A search extract gives 1 per 115 m2 (s.4.2.5); text not opened and the VTC block's membership of the Downtown area is unconfirmed.

parameters.name: Class B and C loading requirement by use, GFA and units
parameters.relationship: More units or GFA triggers extra Class B or C bays in steps. The 2012 text had none under 100 dwellings and one at 100-299 (older); the current table was not opened.

parameters.name: Passenger-space requirement by use (hotel keys, GFA)
parameters.relationship: Required passenger spaces add kerb or on-site bays that compete with active frontage and push drop-off into the lane. A reviewer reports rows exist in Section 5 including hotels; rate, size and triggers are not confirmed.

parameters.name: Loading bay dimensions by class
parameters.relationship: A larger required bay (Class B 10.2 x 3.4 m in a May 2026 extract versus 8.5 x 3.0 x 3.8 m in 2012) enlarges the dock footprint and headroom, pushing the dock deeper into the floor plate.

parameters.name: Class A bicycle rate
parameters.unit: spaces per unit, m2 or room
parameters.relationship: Higher rates enlarge the secured room. Sources conflict: 1.25 per unit and 1 per 500 m2 commercial (Council 2008 via Memon), 1.5-3 per dwelling and 1 per 170 m2 office (vendor). Only the official table can settle it.

parameters.name: Class B (visitor) bicycle rate
parameters.relationship: Triggered at size thresholds (vendor: 6 spaces at 2,000 m2 office). More spaces lengthen the rack frontage near entries, competing with footway width.

parameters.name: Cyclist route and room quality
parameters.relationship: Class A needs a secured room with lockers and showers, reached by a route from the street. Long ramps, small bike lifts or a route crossing the dock add area and conflict. Limits come from the Design Supplement (not opened).

parameters.name: EV-ready and car-share rows
parameters.relationship: Any stalls supplied can carry car-share and EV-outlet obligations that size the electrical room in SYST. Memon (2009) reports car-share rules and e-bike outlets in the by-law, with EV outlets voluntary; current rules not opened.

parameters.name: Accessible and van-accessible parking
parameters.relationship: More parking-using GFA raises accessible stalls; van-accessible stalls need wider aisles and more headroom, enlarging the level plate. Still required after 2024; rate and split not found.

parameters.name: Child-care capacity
parameters.relationship: Adding a child-care facility adds Class A 1 per 17 employees and Class B 1 per 6 FTE spaces, per a June 2024 report extract.

parameters.name: TDM variance and City TDM requirement

modules.name: Transit connection and station-entrance capacity
modules.effort: S for tier 1 (arithmetic, lookup tables, demand scenario); M with GTFS surge inputs; L for agent-based validation (roadmap)
modules.design_question: Can the below-grade secondary station connection carry tower, station and through flows at acceptable space per person and queue area, and what is still unchecked for egress?
inputs: PeakHourDemand transit_in/out from P09-M01 (or P09-M07 adjusted)
Required scenario: station-patron demand captured by the new entrance (TransLink entrance or boardings data, or a user share of station flow) and through-pedestrian flow
Layer 0: polyline or polygon of the connection (stairs, escalators, lifts, fare line) with clear widths
Station location from SITE (City rapid-transit-stations dataset) and GTFS headways for the actual station
User-entered train loads and platform, stair, escalator and gate capacities from TransLink (not public in sources opened)

parameters.name: Clear passage width
parameters.relationship: Wider clear width lowers flow per metre and raises space per pedestrian, moving the link to a better walkway band. Required width equals design flow divided by the flow rate at the chosen band.

parameters.name: Design surge flow per train arrival
parameters.relationship: Alightings per train x entrance share / dispersal time sets the one-to-five-minute surge. Larger platoons from longer headways or bunching worsen the band. Use this instead of hourly flow x surge factor, which double-counts peaking.

parameters.name: Station-patron demand captured by the new entrance
parameters.relationship: A public secondary entrance serves everyone nearby, so its flow can exceed the tower's own demand. More captured station flow lowers space per person and may govern the width. Scenario input; no sourced share.

parameters.name: Through-pedestrian flow
parameters.relationship: Passer-by flow between the plaza, neighbouring sites and the street adds to tower and station flow on the same width and worsens the band. No City pedestrian-count dataset was found.

parameters.name: Entrance choice by walking time
parameters.relationship: Shorter walking time to the new entrance raises its share of station flow. Default is shortest-walk assignment over the passage graph; an optional logit scale is a team assumption. The VTPI mode-choice elasticities are not used here.

parameters.name: Walking speed, counter-flow fraction and effective-width deduction
parameters.relationship: More opposing flow, columns or furniture reduces effective width and lowers speed, raising density. Values come from TCQSM chapter 10, which could not be read, so all are editable assumptions.

parameters.name: Stair, escalator, lift and fare-gate throughput
parameters.relationship: Lower vertical or gate throughput creates queues where the passage meets the platform or fare line. No sourced rates; user-entered from TransLink or TCQSM.

parameters.name: Train headway and train load
parameters.relationship: Shorter headways shrink platoon size and platform crowding. Expo trunk about 2-3 min and Canada Line trunk about 3 min at peak; the Millennium Line does not serve the CBD. Read GTFS for the actual station.

metrics.name: Walkway space per pedestrian on moving links
metrics.good: 1.4 m2 or more (Fruin walkway LOS C or better; editable)
metrics.bad: Below 0.9 m2 (walkway LOS E or worse; editable)
metrics.value_status: unverified (boundaries supplied by reviewer from Fruin 1971; exhibit not read)
metrics.applicability_status: source-stated (TCQSM applies Fruin to station walkways) once read
metrics.basis: 1.4 and 0.9 m2 are walkway-scale boundaries (C/D and D/E), not queuing values. Remaining boundaries to be read from the TCQSM exhibit.
metrics.method: Flow per metre divided by walking speed gives density; invert to space per person; map to the walkway scale.

metrics.name: Queue area per person at stair or fare line (queuing scale)
metrics.good: 0.7 m2 or more (queuing LOS C or better; editable preset)
metrics.bad: Below 0.3 m2 (queuing LOS E or F); 0.3-0.7 shown amber
metrics.value_status: unverified (reviewer scale A 1.2 or more, B 0.9-1.2, C 0.7-0.9, D 0.3-0.7, E 0.2-0.3, F under 0.2; exhibit not read, boundaries such as 0.65 versus 0.7 may differ by edition)
metrics.basis: Replaces the earlier use of walkway boundaries (1.4 and 0.9) for queues.
metrics.method: Queue length from the cumulative diagram times area per person, mapped to the queuing scale.

metrics.name: Required width divided by provided width
metrics.good: 1.0 or less (provided width suffices at the chosen band)
metrics.bad: Above 1.0
metrics.basis: Derived from the chosen walkway band; sized on tower plus station plus through flow.
metrics.method: W_req = design flow / flow rate at chosen band, compared with effective width.

metrics.name: TfL PCL on below-grade passage (removed)
metrics.good: TfL PCL not used underground; used only for street-level footways in P09-M04
metrics.bad: Applying TfL footway bands (B+ 11 ppmm) to station passages, stairs or fare lines
metrics.value_status: sourced (S17 scope is footways and crossings)
metrics.basis: TfL guidance covers footways and crossings only; peak-hour basis; it was misapplied to peak-minute station flows.
metrics.method: Rule: any TfL band used on a link flagged underground is labelled team assumption and cannot produce a badge.

metrics.name: Egress hand-off status
metrics.good: Egress report from SYST (NFPA 130 or authority criteria) attached and accepted by the station owner
metrics.bad: No egress report: all width badges withheld and outputs labelled 'comfort only, not egress-compliant'
metrics.basis: Reviewer: platform-evacuation and point-of-safety criteria may govern width regardless of comfort.
metrics.method: Check for an attached egress record; otherwise watermark all outputs.

visualization: Plan-view false-colour of each passage link by walkway band (A dark green to F red), with legend ticks at the band boundaries and a diagonal 'NOT EGRESS-CHECKED' hatch until a hand-off is attached
Line chart of queue length at the stair or fare line over a 10-minute train-arrival cycle with storage capacity as a dashed line
Stacked bar of entrance load by source (tower, station patrons, through) with the share of each stated
Optional animated agents coloured by local density from JuPedSim trajectories (roadmap)
outputs: PassageCapacityReport {link_id, flow, space_per_person, band, required_width, badge_withheld}
StationEntranceLoad (persons per hour by direction and source) for liaison with the station owner and the policy reflection
ConnectionGeometry (typed polyline with widths) for STRC, SYST and SPAC
EgressHandoff {status, standard, assigned_to: SYST} placeholder
modules.method: 1) Build a passage graph from the Layer 0 centreline; each link gets effective width = clear width minus deductions. 2) Demand = tower transit trips (M01/M07) + station patrons captured by the new entrance + through pedestrians. 3) Surge flow per link = alightings per train x entrance share / dispersal time; entrance share by shortest walking time (optional logit). 4) Density = flow per metre / walking speed; map space per person to the walkway scale. 5) Queues at stairs and fare line from cumulative arrivals minus service over a 10-minute window; area per person mapped to the queuing scale. 6) Required width = flow / flow rate at the chosen band. 7) Outputs carry 'comfort only, not egress-compliant' and no green width badge until an egress record is attached. Optional validation: JuPedSim with PedPy or SUMO.
modules.human_judgment: Agreement with the station owner on entrance location and share of flow, wayfinding and arrival experience, whether the connection is a public amenity or back-of-house shortcut, structural conflicts, accessible route design (CSA B651 checklist), and life-safety egress, which this module does not assess.
modules.limits: Platform and train-load capacity are not computed. Walkway and queuing scales are unverified (TCQSM chapter 10 unread). Egress, fire separation and platform evacuation (NFPA 130 or authority criteria) are out of scope and may govern width. The neighbouring station is hypothetical. For the 30 Nov deadline use a manual check; this tier ships by 10 Dec.

modules.name: Entry flows and street-footway comfort
modules.effort: M (MVP is the street-footway ppmm and Figure 9 lookup; queue and Poisson runs are v1)
modules.design_question: Do entrances, forecourts and adjacent street footways stay comfortable at peak for their TfL area type, and where do queues spill into the public realm?
inputs: PeakHourDemand (walk, transit, taxi arrivals) from P09-M01 or P09-M07
Layer 0: entrance openings (position, clear width, door count) and the program each serves
SITE: footway and forecourt polygons and street classes (arterial, retail high street, lane, transit plaza, mid-block connection)
Optional: pedestrian counts on adjacent footways supplied by the user; optional TfL spreadsheet result for Average of Maximum Activity

parameters.name: Entrance clear width and door count
parameters.relationship: More clear width raises entry service rate and shortens queues. Fewer doors for the same arrivals push the queue out onto the footway. Service rates are team assumptions.

parameters.name: Arrival peaking (15-minute PHF, shift-start alignment)
parameters.relationship: Aligned shift starts concentrate arrivals; a lower PHF (more peaked) raises peak ppmm and queue spill. No sourced Vancouver factor, so it is a preset. This is the traffic-engineering PHF, separate from the K share in P09-M01.

parameters.name: Screening or turnstile throughput
parameters.relationship: Slower screening lowers entry service rate, so queues form earlier. No sourced rate was found.

parameters.name: Footway clear width after furniture and buffers
parameters.relationship: Narrower clear width raises ppmm for through pedestrians plus entering flow. TfL deducts standard wall and kerb buffers and street furniture from clear width.

parameters.name: Background through-flow on the footway
parameters.relationship: More passer-by flow adds to tower flow on the same width and worsens the band. TfL Figure 9 accepts B at peak on a High Street but treats B as at risk for Office and Retail and Transport Interchange.

parameters.name: Area-type mapping of Vancouver street classes
parameters.relationship: Arterial maps to Office and Retail, retail high street to High Street, transit plaza frontage to Transport Interchange, mid-block connection to Office and Retail. A stricter type lowers the permitted ppmm and widens the footway needed. Team assumption.

parameters.name: Queueing area per person in lobby
parameters.relationship: More area per waiting person keeps queues inside the lobby and cuts spill onto the footway. Area standards (Fruin queuing scale) were not read.

parameters.name: Entry share by frontage (arterial, high street, lane)
parameters.relationship: More entries on the retail high street load that footway and lower its band; entries on the lane relieve the frontage but weaken public-facing activity. A design judgement, not a sourced rule.

parameters.name: Taxi and ride-hail drop-off bays
parameters.relationship: More kerb bays shorten vehicle queues in the lane or street but take footway or frontage. Sized with the kerbside model in P09-M05.

metrics.name: Footway PCL at peak by area type (TfL Figure 9)
metrics.unit: ppmm (peak-hour people per hour / 60 / clear width)
metrics.good: B+ or better (11 ppmm or less) for every area type; B (12-14) also accepted on High Street at peak
metrics.bad: C+ or worse (18 ppmm or more), the TfL floor; B- (15-17) at risk; non-integer values between printed bands take the worse band
metrics.applicability_status: team-applied (London guidance; cell-level Figure 9 ratings to be transcribed by two users)
metrics.basis: Replaces the single 11/18 ppmm pair for all area types and the peak-minute basis. Peak-hour flow is the TfL basis.
metrics.method: (peak-hour through-flow + entering flow) / 60 / clear width, looked up by area type in a Figure 9 table with amber bands.

metrics.name: Average of Maximum Activity check
metrics.good: Rated acceptable or better for the area type in the TfL spreadsheet
metrics.bad: Rated unacceptable for the area type
metrics.value_status: unverified (spreadsheet not opened; 10-second maxima not public)
metrics.basis: TfL computes this from busiest 10-second samples built into its spreadsheet; the tool cannot reproduce it, so the user imports the result.
metrics.method: Imported rating shown beside the peak-hour band.

metrics.name: Entrance clear width divided by width required for the target band
metrics.good: 1.0 or more
metrics.bad: Below 1.0
metrics.basis: Derived from the chosen band's upper ppmm (11 for B+).
metrics.method: Provided width / (peak-hour flow / 60 / band upper limit).

metrics.name: Queue spill outside the property line
metrics.good: 0 m2 at design peak
metrics.bad: More than 0 m2
metrics.basis: Editable preset; no source.
metrics.method: Queue area beyond lobby polygon intersected with forecourt or footway polygon.

metrics.name: 95th-percentile screening wait
metrics.good: 2 min or less
metrics.bad: More than 5 min
metrics.basis: Editable preset; no source.
metrics.method: Poisson arrivals, 200 replications.

visualization: Ground-plane heat-map of predicted ppmm on footways and forecourt using the TfL A+ to E legend, with the area type printed on each segment and entry arrows scaled to flow
Entry badges showing band and area-type rating (comfortable, acceptable, at risk, unacceptable) linked to the Figure 9 lookup
Small-multiple queue-length time series per entry with the lobby capacity line
Spill polygons outlined red where the queue exceeds the lobby
outputs: EntryFlowMatrix (entry x minute, in/out)
SpilloverPolygons for PUBL modules and SPAC
FootwayPCL by segment and area type for human-scale scoring
TaxiTNC kerb demand for P09-M05
modules.method: Assign each entry its arrivals per minute from PeakHourDemand using a program-to-entry map and a 15-minute PHF. For each footway segment add through-flow and tower flow, divide people per hour by 60 and by clear width (width minus buffers) to get peak-hour ppmm, then look up the band and the Figure 9 rating for the segment's area type (street class mapped as a team assumption). Values between printed bands take the worse band; any segment at C+ or worse fails regardless of vitality. Entry service capacity = clear width x ppmm at the chosen band, or the turnstile rate; a cumulative-arrival and service diagram gives queue length, converted to area; overflow beyond the lobby polygon spills to the forecourt or footway. Optional Poisson run (200 replications) gives the 95th-percentile queue. Station passages are handled in P09-M03, not here.
modules.human_judgment: Entry sequence and sense of welcome, whether queues are acceptable as gathering space, cultural protocols for arrival and gathering, security stance, activation of ground-floor edges, and balancing comfort bands against an intimate street character.
modules.limits: TfL bands are calibrated to London footways and crossings, not Vancouver or interior spaces. No City pedestrian-count dataset was found, so through-flow must be supplied or assumed. Peaking, screening and service rates are unsourced presets. Static peak only; events and weather are not modelled. Figure 9 cells need two-person transcription from the PDF.

modules.name: Servicing, kerbside and access placement
modules.effort: M for placement checks, Erlang sizing and the design-vehicle library; L for swept-path analysis (v1)
modules.design_question: Can deliveries, passenger drop-off and servicing be handled from lanes and kerbs with enough bays and storage that trucks do not queue onto streets or cross the retail high street?
inputs: Layer 0: massing, program, core and ground-floor footprint
SITE: block edges with street class (arterial, retail high street, lane), mid-block connections and lane width
LoadingBayCount and PassengerSpaceCount from P09-M02
Optional DockScheduleDemand from P09-M06 (preset if absent)
Taxi and ride-hail kerb demand from P09-M01 and P09-M04
City open data: lanes, one-way streets, bikeways, truck routes, right-of-way widths

parameters.name: Number of loading bays c (by class)
parameters.relationship: More bays lower utilisation and the probability that an arriving truck waits (Erlang C). Stability requires arrival rate below c times service rate.

parameters.name: Truck arrival rate lambda in the busiest hour
parameters.relationship: Rises with retail, hotel and residential GFA and unit count, and raises utilisation and queue length. No sourced Vancouver or freight-trip-generation rate was found, so it is an editable preset.

parameters.name: Dwell time per truck
parameters.relationship: Longer dwell (move-ins, bulk deliveries) raises utilisation in proportion; consolidation or booking shortens it.

parameters.name: Design vehicle by loading class (library)
parameters.relationship: A larger design vehicle needs a longer bay, wider turning area, more headroom and a deeper dock. The library maps each class to a TAC design vehicle plus the City refuse truck; dimensions are transcribed by the user.

parameters.name: Access position along the lane (distance from nearest intersection)
parameters.relationship: Closer to the intersection leaves less on-site storage for waiting trucks, so queues spill onto the street sooner. No Vancouver spacing standard was obtained.

parameters.name: Vehicle-access frontage by street class
parameters.relationship: More access width on the retail high street breaks the retail edge and adds conflict points; lane access protects the public realm but loads the lane. The 1997 plan sought better truck access to downtown lanes.

parameters.name: Lane width and turning radii for the design vehicle
parameters.relationship: Narrower lanes or smaller radii raise the setback or turntable needed to enter the dock. City datasets give legal right-of-way widths only, so lane width is a required input, defaulted to a flagged team assumption.

parameters.name: Dock clear height and ramp slope
parameters.relationship: Taller design vehicles need more structure and floor-to-floor height at dock level. By-law envelope values are in the 2012/2026 text and the 1988 supplement, none opened.

parameters.name: Kerb demand: passenger loading, taxi, ride-hail, courier, accessible drop-off
parameters.relationship: The larger of by-law passenger spaces (P09-M02) and queue-model demand governs. More kerb bays on the high street break active frontage; lane bays load the lane. Frontage is allocated across arterial, high street and lane.

parameters.name: Number of curb cuts crossing footways
parameters.relationship: Each added crossing adds a pedestrian-vehicle conflict point and lowers footway comfort and safety along that frontage.

metrics.name: Dock utilisation rho = lambda / (c x mu)
metrics.good: Below 0.70 (preset)
metrics.bad: 1.0 or more (queue grows without bound)
metrics.basis: Instability at rho of 1 or more is queueing theory; the 0.70 comfort level is a preset.
metrics.method: Arrival rate over service capacity.

metrics.name: Probability that a truck must wait (Erlang C)
metrics.good: 0.10 or less
metrics.bad: More than 0.30
metrics.basis: Editable presets; formula from S22.
metrics.method: Erlang C formula.

metrics.name: 95th-percentile truck queue versus on-site storage
metrics.good: Queue no longer than on-site storage
metrics.bad: Queue longer than storage (spills onto street or lane)
metrics.basis: Geometric logic; storage length from the plan.
metrics.method: SimPy run with lognormal dwell.

metrics.name: Vehicle access on the retail high street
metrics.good: 0 m
metrics.bad: Any curb cut on that frontage
metrics.basis: Preset; Vancouver downtown lane-access guidance was not opened.
metrics.method: Sum of access widths by edge class.

metrics.name: Swept-path clearance for the library design vehicle
metrics.good: Design-vehicle envelope clears all structure and lane edges
metrics.bad: Any intersection of envelope and obstruction
metrics.basis: Geometric test; clearance margin editable; envelope is a simplified kinematic sweep.
metrics.method: Shapely intersection of swept envelope with obstacles.

metrics.name: Kerb bays provided versus the larger of by-law passenger spaces and queue-model demand
metrics.good: 1.0 or more
metrics.bad: Below 1.0
metrics.basis: Passenger-loading rule rows are not confirmed; queue demand is a preset.
metrics.method: Provided bays divided by max(required, modelled demand).

visualization: Block plan with edges coloured by street class and candidate access points as pins: green on lane, amber on side street, red on high street; designated truck routes drawn as a heavy line
Swept-path polygons for each library design vehicle over the dock plan, red fill where the envelope hits structure
Bar chart of probability of waiting versus number of bays with the design point and thresholds marked
Gantt strip of dock occupancy across the day with queue length overlay, and a kerb-allocation strip per frontage (passenger, taxi, courier, accessible)
outputs: ServicingPlan {access_points[], bay_assignments[], P_wait, queue_p95, conflict_points[]}
KerbAllocation by frontage for PUBL
FrontageOccupancy by street class for PUBL
DockFootprint and ramp envelope for STRC and SPAC
ServicingVehicleSchedule for P09-M08
modules.method: Placement: classify every block edge from SITE (lane, arterial, high street), list candidate access points, and score them by street class and distance from the intersection. Sizing: treat the dock as an M/M/c queue with arrival rate lambda and mean dwell 1/mu; compute utilisation, Erlang C probability of waiting and Wq = C/(c mu - lambda). A SimPy run with lognormal dwell gives the 95th-percentile queue for comparison with storage. Geometry: pick the design vehicle for each loading class from the library (TAC designations plus City refuse truck), sweep its envelope along the entry path with a minimum turning radius and the required lane width, and intersect with lane edges, columns and ramps using Shapely. Kerb bays = larger of by-law passenger spaces and queue demand. Count curb cuts and conflict points per frontage and rank access options.
modules.human_judgment: Where servicing sits relative to the public realm and the lane's character, whether lanes become activated shared spaces, operating regime (booking, hours), neighbour effects, and how much conflict is acceptable against a larger dock footprint.
modules.limits: Arrival rates, dwell times and thresholds are presets; no sourced freight-trip rates were found. Lane widths are not in City data. The design-vehicle library is empty until a user transcribes TAC values. Swept path is a simplified kinematic envelope, not certified vehicle tracking. By-law envelopes came from unopened pages and need checking.

modules.name: Waste, recycling and move-in logistics (experimental)
modules.effort: M (experimental until City storage guidance and generation rates are attached)
modules.design_question: How do garbage, recycling and organics storage, vertical transfer and move-in options compare, without conflicting with deliveries or public frontages? Relative comparison only; no pass/fail.
inputs: Layer 0: program GFA, dwelling units, hotel keys, food and retail GFA
Layer 0: core, service lift and waste-room tags with heights
LoadingBayCount from P09-M02
User-selected collection frequency and container types

parameters.name: Waste generation rate by use
parameters.unit: kg or m3 per day per 100 m2, unit or room
parameters.relationship: Higher rates raise storage volume, container count and pickups. No Vancouver or Metro Vancouver rate was opened, so values are editable placeholders and only relative comparisons are shown.

parameters.name: Stream split (food waste, recyclable paper, corrugated cardboard, containers, beverage containers, clean wood, polystyrene, garbage)
parameters.relationship: Each banned stream needs its own container and room area, so more streams raise area and handling trips while garbage volume falls. The stream list is from Metro Vancouver's ban list; the shares are placeholders.

parameters.name: Collection frequency
parameters.relationship: More frequent pickup reduces storage volume but raises truck visits at the dock.

parameters.name: Container type and footprint
parameters.relationship: Larger containers cut handling trips but need wider doors, more headroom and heavier truck access.

parameters.name: Vertical transfer method (chute, service lift, other)
parameters.relationship: Taller buildings make chutes or dedicated service lifts more necessary. Ties to vertical transportation in SYST. Used for relative comparison of options.

parameters.name: Move-in and move-out events
parameters.relationship: Events = units x turnover rate. Higher turnover (rental, short stay) raises freight-lift and dock bookings, peaking at month-end.

parameters.name: Freight lift car and door size
parameters.relationship: Smaller cars lengthen move times and restrict furniture. Sized in SYST; lift standards were not opened.

parameters.name: Dock hours available per day

modules.name: Transportation demand management scenarios
modules.effort: S (tier 1 measure table and scaling; Monte Carlo is optional)
modules.design_question: Which TDM measures could this tower credibly adopt, how far could they cut auto trips and parking demand from a CBD baseline, and what by-law relief might they support?
inputs: ModeShareSummary and PeakHourDemand from P09-M01
ParkingLoadingBikeLedger from P09-M02
User-selected TDM measures and intensity (subsidy %, parking price, and so on)
Layer 0: end-of-trip facilities (bike rooms, showers) and car-share stalls
City TDM requirement row (plan, measures or points, financial security) with version date, status 'unverified pending the City bulletin'

parameters.name: Transit or rideshare subsidy level
parameters.relationship: Higher subsidy lowers commute auto trips. A model predicted -35% commute travel in CBDs for a 100% subsidy and -20% for 50% (Sacramento model, predicted not observed, baseline not stated).

parameters.name: Parking price or cash-out
parameters.relationship: Higher price lowers driving: elasticity -0.1 to -0.3, so a 10% rise cuts driving 1-3%. Commuter cash-out reduces automobile commuting 15-25%. Evidence is from car-oriented contexts.

parameters.name: Cost-recovery (full-price) parking
parameters.relationship: Moving from free to cost-based parking reduces parking demand 10-30% and drive-alone commuting 10-30% in the evidence base; the effect shrinks where parking is already priced and auto share is low.

parameters.name: Programme bundle (information, services, incentives)
parameters.relationship: Comprehensive worksite bundles cut 4-20% of peak auto trips (Rye 2002; Boarnet et al. 2014); US survey bundles with incentives about 15% versus about 7% for information only; programmes without financial incentives usually under 10%.

parameters.name: Shared parking and unbundling
parameters.relationship: Sharing lets 20-40% more users per space. Each management measure typically trims requirements 10-30%, a full package 30-50%; TDM buildings in Minneapolis-St Paul needed 17-24% fewer spaces than ITE rates imply.

parameters.name: End-of-trip facilities and car-share
parameters.relationship: Secure Class A rooms, showers and car-share stalls support cycling and low-car living. The City has required car-share since at least 2009. No quantified effect found; used as qualitative toggles.

parameters.name: Evidence baseline auto share and scaling factor k
parameters.relationship: Published reductions come from car-oriented baselines. Apply them scaled by k = site auto share / evidence auto share (capped at 1), so a low-auto CBD site gets a smaller claim. Evidence auto share is an editable team assumption.

parameters.name: Overlap discount between measures
parameters.relationship: Measure effects overlap, so summing overstates results. The combined reduction is capped at the scaled evidence range for the chosen bundle type, not added.

parameters.name: Delivery consolidation
parameters.relationship: Fewer, consolidated deliveries lower arrival rate lambda and dock utilisation in P09-M05. No sourced percentage was found.

metrics.name: Claimed reduction in peak-hour auto-driver commute trips (scaled by k)
metrics.good: 4-20% multiplied by k (comprehensive worksite bundles); evidence context: US metro, mostly predicted
metrics.bad: Above 37% multiplied by k (highest office result cited, measured against ITE rates); the band between 20% and 37% is amber
metrics.applicability_status: team-applied (US and Minneapolis-St Paul baselines, not a transit-rich CBD)
metrics.basis: Corrects treating VTPI ranges as verified thresholds for a downtown Vancouver tower. Ewing 35% is a prediction; 34-37% is relative to ITE rates.
metrics.method: Compare capped combined effect with scaled evidence bands; show the evidence context beside each value.

metrics.name: Claimed parking-demand reduction (scaled by k)
metrics.good: 30% or less (typical per measure 10-30%) multiplied by k
metrics.bad: Above 50% (top of the 30-50% package range) multiplied by k
metrics.basis: VTPI parking-management ranges applied to a CBD baseline are team-applied.
metrics.method: Adjusted parking demand versus baseline, scaled by k.

metrics.name: Financial-incentive content of the bundle
metrics.good: At least one price, cash-out or subsidy measure included
metrics.bad: Information-only bundle (about 7% effect in the US survey)
metrics.value_status: sourced (S19 Best Workplaces for Commuters survey)
metrics.basis: Survey figures as cited by VTPI under conservative assumptions.
metrics.method: Check measure list for incentive types.

metrics.name: City TDM requirement met (policy view)
metrics.good: Required plan elements present once the City row is loaded and checked
metrics.bad: Row missing or unchecked: result shown as 'City policy view not verified'
metrics.basis: Storeys reports the TDM policy was tied to the removed minimums and staff plan to lower financial expectations downtown.
metrics.method: Rule-pack row check; reported beside the evidence view.

visualization: Waterfall from baseline auto-driver trips through each measure to the adjusted value, whiskers for low-high effect, a red band beyond the scaled 37% limit and an 'evidence context' label on each bar
Before-and-after stacked mode-share bars with the City target as a context line
Evidence table: measure, effect range, source badge, status colour, predicted versus observed, evidence region
Line chart of parking demand versus stalls supplied
outputs: AdjustedModeSplit and PeakHourDemand_TDM for P09-M03, M04 and M08
ParkingDemandAdjusted for P09-M02
TDMPlan (measures, effects, sources, City-policy row status) for the policy-reflection board

modules.method: Start from baseline auto-driver commute trips and parking demand in P09-M01. For each selected measure take low, central and high effect values from the cited ranges (table with source ids and evidence region). Scale each effect by k = site auto share / evidence auto share (cap 1). Combine multiplicatively with an overlap discount, then cap at the scaled evidence range of the chosen bundle type. Apply the reduction to commute trips only; visitor and servicing trips are unchanged. Recompute auto-driver trips, parking demand and the Class A bicycle uplift, and report the parking and loading relief that could be argued in a variance next to the City TDM row. Output a TDM plan skeleton. An optional 1,000-draw Monte Carlo between low and high values gives a spread labelled as scenario spread.
modules.human_judgment: Which measures fit the operator and tenants, commitments the design team will make, equity of parking pricing and subsidies, and whether to argue for a by-law variance.
modules.limits: Effect sizes are predictions or US results measured against car-oriented baselines, so they are scaled and never added. They apply to commute trips only. The City TDM policy for rezonings, tied to the removed minimums, was not opened. Measures need an operator; the tool cannot enforce commitments.

modules.design_question: What do the tower's vehicle, servicing and drop-off trips add to adjacent intersections and lanes at peak, and where do queues or conflicts reach pedestrians, cyclists or transit?

ServicingPlan access points and truck schedule from P09-M05
Optional: pedestrian band results from P09-M04
Street network from OpenStreetMap (OSMnx) and City open data (public streets, lanes, one-way streets, bikeways, truck routes)
User-supplied background volumes, signal timings, 15-minute PHF and lane geometry
Rapid-transit stations and lines

parameters.name: Added peak-hour vehicle volume by approach
parameters.relationship: Higher added volume raises v/c and control delay at the receiving intersection, moving LOS toward E or F as critical v/c approaches 0.85 to 1.0.

parameters.name: Signal cycle length and green split
parameters.relationship: More green for the loaded movement raises its capacity and cuts its delay. Effects on pedestrian waiting are a design judgement to check in P09-M04.

parameters.name: Trip distribution to approaches (set by access position)
parameters.relationship: Access on a lane near an arterial pushes more turns onto that intersection; access on a side street spreads turns but loads a quieter street.

parameters.name: Background traffic, growth and 15-minute PHF
parameters.relationship: Higher background volume or a more peaked PHF leaves less spare capacity, so the same tower trips cause a larger delay increase. City counts are historical or link-only.

parameters.name: Pedestrian and cyclist crossing volumes
parameters.relationship: More crossings at a curb cut or intersection raise conflict exposure and cut vehicle capacity during crossing phases.

parameters.name: Bikeway type on adjacent streets
parameters.relationship: Protected or AAA bikeways beside access points add conflict points and may need driveway redesign. The bikeways dataset carries type and AAA flags.

parameters.name: Taxi, ride-hail and delivery vehicle share
parameters.relationship: More ride-hail and delivery vehicles raise kerb occupancy and add trips even when parking supply is small. Scales with P09-M01 and P09-M05 outputs.

parameters.name: Transit stations and frequency near the site
parameters.relationship: Nearby rapid-transit stations and short headways support a higher transit share in P09-M01. The City dataset gives 22 station points; headways come from GTFS for Expo and Canada lines.

metrics.name: Intersection control delay (LOS)
metrics.good: 55 s or less (LOS A-D)
metrics.bad: Above 80 s (LOS F), or any lane group with v/c above 1.0; 55-80 s (LOS E) shown amber
metrics.value_status: sourced (S18 Table 3-3, HCM 2000); v/c override expert-stated and unverified
metrics.applicability_status: team-applied (LOS D as acceptable is a team choice)
metrics.basis: Delay bands match FHWA Table 3-3; the v/c above 1.0 gives LOS F rule is reported for later HCM editions and is not in S18. Vancouver ranks walking, cycling and transit first.
metrics.method: Control delay from signal timing and volumes, then banded; label 'HCM-style (bands unchanged in later editions, unverified)'.

metrics.name: Critical volume-to-capacity ratio
metrics.good: Below 0.85 (under capacity)
metrics.bad: Above 1.00 (demand exceeds capacity); 0.85-0.95 near capacity (amber), 0.95-1.00 unstable flow (red-amber)
metrics.value_status: sourced (S18 Table 3-2, Quick Estimation Method, HCM 2000 edition)
metrics.basis: Corrects the earlier single 0.85-1.00 band: Table 3-2 splits near capacity (0.85-0.95) from unstable flow (0.95-1.00). Edition currency vs later HCM not checked.
metrics.method: Volume over capacity for the critical movement, banded with Table 3-2.

metrics.name: Queue spill from the site access onto the street
metrics.good: 0 m
metrics.bad: Any spill
metrics.basis: Geometric preset; storage from P09-M05.
metrics.method: Simulated 95th-percentile queue minus storage length.

metrics.name: Mode-priority check
metrics.good: No mitigation worsens pedestrian band, cycling or transit access in order to cut vehicle delay
metrics.bad: Any such trade-off
metrics.value_status: sourced (1997 hierarchy as reported by Memon 2009)
metrics.basis: The 1997 hierarchy (pedestrians, cyclists, transit, goods, then cars) may be superseded.
metrics.method: Compare P09-M04 bands and bikeway conflicts before and after mitigation.

visualization: Map with street edges coloured by v/c on a diverging 0-1.2 scale with ticks at 0.85, 0.95 and 1.0, and intersections as discs sized by delay and coloured by LOS A (green) to F (red)
Difference map (with minus without project) of delay in seconds
deck.gl animated trips layer for simulation output with queue bars at site access (roadmap tier)
Mode-priority panel showing pedestrian bands, bikeway conflicts and transit delay beside vehicle LOS
Chord diagram of project trips by origin zone and mode
outputs: IntersectionPerformance {id, volume, v/c, delay, LOS} with and without project
NetworkFlowDelta (GeoJSON edges)
QueueSpillFlags for P09-M05 and PUBL
SimulationConfig (SUMO files) for reuse by forks
modules.method: Tier 1, static: distribute project peak-hour vehicle trips onto approaches using access positions and shortest paths on the OSM network; add background volumes; compute v/c per movement from saturation flow and green split and delay with HCM-style terms using user timings; classify delay with the FHWA/HCM bands and apply the LOS F override where lane-group v/c exceeds 1.0 (expert-stated, unverified). Tier 2, simulation (roadmap): export network and demand to SUMO (netconvert) or UXsim and read edge delays and queues from detectors, with-project versus without-project. A mode-priority check reads pedestrian bands from P09-M04 and flags mitigation that trades pedestrian comfort for vehicle delay. The 15-minute PHF is an explicit input. Every input shows provenance and status colour; placeholder signal data are labelled.
modules.human_judgment: How much vehicle delay to accept against pedestrian, cycle and transit priority, whether to propose street changes, how to narrate impact in the policy reflection, and whether assumed signal timings are credible.
modules.limits: City data are link-only intersection counts (2020) and 2004-2013 counters in a legacy tool; no signal timings or lane widths. HCM is paywalled, so delay formulas are generic and the HCM 2000 bands may differ from later editions. The site is hypothetical, so trips are scenario inputs. Microsimulation needs calibration; results are comparative and not a traffic impact study.

flags.claim: Downtown Vancouver, or any Vancouver site, must provide a minimum number of off-street parking spaces.
flags.correction: No minimum parking applies for any use citywide since 30 June 2024; the downtown peninsula was exempt from 2018. Accessible, visitor, bicycle and loading spaces are still required.
flags.detail: Sources S01 and S02 (opened) agree. The Province's TOA rules also bar required residential parking near rapid transit (S24). The tool must never score a parking shortfall as a deficiency.

flags.claim: The 2023 Trip Diary weekday shares for CBD sub-regions 21 and 22 are the right default mode split for all trips the tower generates (office, retail, hotel, residential).
flags.correction: Use residence-based shares for residential trips and destination-based shares (trips ending in the CBD: Census place-of-work, City cordon counts or a dashboard destination filter) for attraction uses. Store basis, sample size and confidence interval with each loaded share and block attraction runs on a residence-based share.
flags.detail: The survey recruits and weights households by residence sub-area (S15 weighting exhibit uses household and person controls by sub seed; sub-regions 21 and 22 have household sample targets of a few hundred each). The shares therefore describe trips by CBD residents, not workers and visitors arriving from across the region. Evidence: S15 (opened, text extracted); S16 lists no destination-based product.

flags.claim: TfL Pedestrian Comfort Level bands are verified thresholds for peak-minute flows in below-grade station passages, with B+ (11 ppmm or less) good and 18 ppmm or more bad for all area types.
flags.correction: Use TfL only for street footways, on peak-hour flow (people per hour / 60 / clear width), against the Figure 9 acceptability table by area type, with PCL never below C+ at peak. Use station methods (TCQSM chapter 10 walkway and queuing scales) for passages, stairs and fare lines. Status: team_assumption.
flags.detail: S17 (opened, text extracted): scope is footways and crossings; ppmm is people per hour divided by 60 and by clear width, calculated for average, peak-hour and Average of Maximum Activity flows; Figure 9 treats B as acceptable at peak only on High Street and at risk for Office and Retail and Transport Interchange (cell-level reading to be confirmed); C+ is the floor even where vitality compensates. Multiplying hourly flow by a platoon factor and reading hour-average bands double-counts peaking.

flags.claim: Queue area per person of 1.4 m2 or more is Fruin LOS A-C and below 0.9 m2 is LOS E-F at stairs and fare lines.
flags.correction: 1.4 and 0.9 m2 per person are walkway-scale boundaries (C/D and D/E). Queues use a separate queuing-area scale (reviewer: A 1.2 or more, B 0.9-1.2, C 0.7-0.9, D 0.3-0.7, E 0.2-0.3, F under 0.2 m2 per person). Keep both scales and cite the exhibit once read.
flags.detail: Reviewer expert knowledge of Fruin (1971) as reproduced in TCQSM 3rd ed. ch.10. The primary copy could not be opened (S44 reader page has no table text; the PDF exceeds the fetch size limit), so both scales stay unverified and bounds such as 0.65 versus 0.7 m2 may differ by edition.

flags.claim: Peak headways relevant to the station are Expo 2-5 min, Millennium 3-4 min and Canada 6 min.
flags.correction: For a CBD station use the Expo trunk (about 2-3 min combined) and the Canada Line trunk (about 3 min combined), read from GTFS for the actual station. The Millennium Line terminates at VCC-Clark and is excluded.
flags.detail: S23 (re-opened): Expo 2-5 min is the line's own frequency and 2-3 min combined on shared track; Millennium runs VCC-Clark to Lafarge Lake-Douglas and is not shown serving Waterfront since 2016; Canada Line 6 min is its own branch frequency and 3 min combined on the trunk. The table is hard to parse, so GTFS is authoritative.

flags.claim: FHWA Table 3-2 gives v/c bands of under 0.85 stable, 0.85-1.00 near capacity and over 1.00 oversaturated.
flags.correction: Cite Table 3-2 exactly: under 0.85, 0.85-0.95 near capacity, 0.95-1.00 unstable flow, over 1.00 demand exceeds capacity. The single 0.85-1.00 band is from section 3.3.5. Add the reviewer-stated LOS F override for lane-group v/c above 1.0 (later HCM editions; unverified) and label the method HCM-style.
flags.detail: S18 re-opened this round: Table 3-2 lists under 0.85, 0.85-0.95, 0.95-1.00 and over 1.00 (HCM 2000 Quick Estimation Method). The page does not map v/c above 1.0 to LOS F; Table 3-3 assigns LOS F by delay above 80 s only.

flags.claim: VTPI TDM reduction ranges (4-20%, about 15%, 34-37%, 35%) are verified thresholds for claimed reductions at a downtown Vancouver tower.
flags.correction: Treat them as team-applied evidence ranges, applied against a car-oriented baseline or scaled by remaining auto share (k), with an 'evidence context: US metro / predicted' label on each value.
flags.detail: S19 re-opened: the 35% and 20% figures are Ewing 1993 Sacramento model predictions; 34-37% is measured against ITE average trip rates in Minneapolis-St Paul (Spack and Finkelstein 2014); 4-20% is Rye and Boarnet worksite programmes; 15% versus 7% is a four-metro US survey. None is measured against a transit-rich CBD baseline, so applying them unscaled double-counts the downtown effect.

flags.claim: ITE trip rates do not consider location, so local survey data are the only option for downtown sites.
flags.correction: ITE is paywalled but, per the reviewer, recent editions classify data by site setting (including Center City Core and Dense Multi-Use Urban) and report person trips; use as an optional cross-check where a user holds a licence.
flags.detail: S46 (Wikipedia) repeats the older wording. The reviewer states the setting categories from practitioner knowledge; ITE pages could not be opened (404, S54), so this correction is unverified.

flags.claim: Downtown maximum for non-residential parking is 1 space per 115 m2 GFA (s.4.2.5).
flags.detail: Seen only in a search-engine extract of the June 2026 Section 4, which could not be opened (bot challenge). Whether the hypothetical VTC block falls inside the by-law's Downtown area is also unconfirmed. A residential maximum row exists in the schema, unpopulated.

flags.claim: Loading rules: Class A, B and C requirements by use and GFA, and bay dimensions (Class B 8.5 x 3.0 x 3.8 m in 2012; 10.2 x 3.4 m in a May 2026 extract).
flags.detail: Section 5 and the Design Supplement could not be opened (Section 5 re-tried once, HTTP 403). The 1988 supplement has a 'superseded' copy. The 2003 and 2012 residential thresholds (none under 100 dwellings) are old. Load the current table by hand through the rule pack.

flags.claim: Bicycle parking rates (dwelling 1.5/2.5/3 per unit by size; office 1 per 170 m2; retail 1 per 340 m2; hotel 1 per 30 units; Class B minima).
flags.detail: Only from a vendor's partial list (S13). Another vendor claims 1.25 per dwelling (S14), and Memon (S12, opened) reports Council approved 1.25 per unit and 1 per 500 m2 commercial in 2008. The Feb 2026 Section 6 was not opened. Treat all as placeholders until the official table is loaded.

flags.claim: City of Vancouver sustainable-mode target of two-thirds of trips and any newer 2050 target.
flags.detail: Transportation 2040, the climate plan and the Vancouver Plan were not opened (vancouver.ca returns HTTP 403). The reviewer notes the target is city-wide and may have a 2030 year in a later plan. The 1997 plan targets in Memon 2009 are historical. Shown as context, not pass/fail.

flags.claim: 2023 Trip Diary mode shares for CBD sub-regions 21 and 22.
flags.detail: The technical report (opened) contains no results; shares exist only in TransLink's Tableau dashboard (S16), are residence-based, and whether a destination filter exists is unconfirmed. Users must read and enter values with basis, sample size and date accessed.

flags.claim: Queuing-area and walkway LOS scales (Fruin) used for stair, fare-line and passage checks.
flags.detail: Reviewer-supplied boundaries (walkway C/D 1.4 and D/E 0.9 m2 per person; queuing A 1.2 or more through F under 0.2) are not read from a primary copy. TCQSM chapter 10 (S44) returned no table text. Stair, escalator and fare-gate throughputs remain unsourced. Keep unverified until read.

flags.claim: The VTC site lies inside a Provincial Transit-Oriented Area.
flags.detail: The TOA page (S24) says 104 areas exist within 800 m of rapid transit, but Vancouver's list was not read, and the site is hypothetical. If it applies, residential parking cannot be required there.

flags.claim: The 1997 Higher Buildings Policy still governs tall-building criteria and has not been replaced by the Review.
flags.detail: The Shape Your City page (S47, opened) says the City is reviewing the policy, with Phase 1 in spring-summer 2026 and adoption expected spring 2027, so the 1997 policy has not been replaced. The policy PDFs (S42, S43) returned HTTP 403, and the page names no transportation criteria. Parking By-law No. 6059 remains the governing instrument for parking, loading and bicycle spaces.

flags.claim: City of Vancouver TDM requirement for developments after the June 2024 parking-minimum removal.
flags.detail: Storeys (S02, opened) reports the TDM policy 'is tied to the minimum parking requirements, which now no longer exist' and staff intend to lower financial expectations in Downtown, Broadway Plan area and TOAs. The City bulletin was not opened; the c. 2021 memo (S11) predates the change, so the TDM-variance logic may be superseded. Carried as a rule row 'unverified pending the City bulletin'.

flags.claim: Emergency egress criteria (NFPA 130 or the authority's rail-station rules) may govern passage and stair width in the station connection regardless of comfort.
flags.detail: Reviewer statement; NFPA 130 (S52) page returned only its title. M03 withholds green width badges and labels outputs 'comfort only, not egress-compliant' until an egress record from SYST is attached.

flags.claim: EV-charging and car-share provisions in the Parking By-law rule pack.
flags.detail: The reviewer said Memon documents EV outlets in the by-law. Memon (S12, opened) actually reports car-share requirements and electrical outlets for electric-assisted bicycles in the by-law, with EV-car outlets described as voluntary or project-specific (East Fraserlands 20%). Current EV rules may sit in the Vancouver Building By-law; rows are loaded as unverified.

flags.claim: Whether the Parking By-law requires passenger loading spaces and at what rate.
flags.detail: No extract captured a passenger-loading clause; a reviewer reports Section 5 includes passenger-space rows by use including hotels. M02 carries passenger-space row types as 'unverified - load from Section 5', and M05 sizes kerb bays as the larger of by-law rows and queue-model demand.

flags.claim: Destination-based mode shares for office, retail, hotel and civic attraction trips to the CBD.
flags.detail: Candidate sources: Statistics Canada 2021 place-of-work tables (S51, HTTP 403, COVID-affected), City downtown cordon counts (cited in S12; no open dataset found), a TransLink dashboard destination filter (unconfirmed). No values are loaded; M01 blocks attraction runs without them.

flags.claim: Servicing, waste and entry presets: truck arrival rates, dwell times, waste generation, container sizes, screening rates, arrival peaking, utilisation and wait thresholds.
flags.detail: No sourced Vancouver values were found. All appear as editable team-assumption badges and become verified only when a user attaches a source. M06 is experimental and shows relative comparisons only.

flags.claim: TfL Pedestrian Comfort Levels (London footways, 2010) are an acceptable threshold system for Vancouver street footways, mapped to TfL area types.
flags.detail: B+ as the recommended minimum and the Figure 9 acceptability grid are TfL rules, not City of Vancouver standards. The street-class to area-type mapping (arterial to Office and Retail, high street to High Street, transit plaza to Transport Interchange) is a team choice. Not used for station passages. Teams may substitute another comfort scale.

flags.claim: LOS D is the acceptable level for vehicle delay at downtown intersections.
flags.detail: LOS delay bands are sourced (S18), but acceptability is a choice. The City ranks walking, cycling and transit above cars, so a poorer vehicle LOS may be justified.

flags.claim: Internal capture is OFF by default in CBD mode and station-entrance choice uses shortest walking time.
flags.detail: Tool design choices to avoid double-discounting trips already in the zone shares (reviewer) and to avoid using mode-choice elasticities for entrance choice. Optional logit scale and NCHRP 684 pair rates are user entries.

unresolved_relationships: Destination-based CBD mode shares by purpose (office, retail, hotel, civic): no loaded source; Census place-of-work and cordon counts not opened.
Share of station flow captured by a new secondary entrance versus walking time and entrance count: no source; the VTPI elasticities describe mode choice, not entrance choice.
Egress width criteria (NFPA 130 or authority rules) for the below-grade connection versus comfort width: standard not opened.
Stair, escalator, lift and fare-gate throughput versus width, and the Fruin walkway and queuing exhibit values: TCQSM chapter 10 returned no text.
Passenger loading requirement versus hotel keys or GFA: no clause located.
Dock count and truck arrival rate versus GFA by use under the 2024-2026 by-law: no sourced freight-trip rate for Vancouver mixed-use towers (freight trip generation research not opened).
Internal capture rate versus use-pair mix: NCHRP 684 not opened, so pair rates are unknown and the method suits ITE vehicle trips.
City TDM requirement (plan, points or measures, financial security) after June 2024 and its link to loading and bicycle variances: bulletin not opened.
Transferability of published TDM effects to a transit-rich CBD baseline: scaling by auto share (k) is a design choice; the evidence auto share is unsourced.
Combined effect of several TDM measures: VTPI gives ranges but no overlap formula, so the cap rule is a design choice.
Waste and recycling generation per m2 or unit, container and room standards: only the Metro Vancouver banned-stream list was opened; City storage guidance not opened.
Pedestrian arrival peaking versus staggered shift starts at office entries: no sourced factor.
Effect of lane access position and lane width on queue spill and swept path: no Vancouver spacing or lane-width standard; City datasets give only legal right-of-way widths.
Design-vehicle dimensions and turning radii by loading class and the City refuse truck: TAC Geometric Design Guide not opened.
